content: Glycine N-methyltransferase (GNMT) is an enzyme encoded by the GNMT gene in humans. It was first described in 1960 by Blumenstein and Williams in guinea pig liver. However, the enzyme was not purified until 1972, when Kerr isolated it from rabbit liver. In 1984, Cook and Wagner demonstrated that a liver cytosolic folate-binding protein is identical to GNMT. The human GNMT gene was cloned in 2000 by Chen and colleagues. GNMT constitutes 3% to 9% of the soluble protein in the liver. Beyond the liver, GNMT activity has been identified in other tissues, including the pancreas and kidney. It is most abundant in the peri-portal region of the liver and the exocrine tissue of the pancreas. GNMT proteins are also found in tissues actively involved in secretion, such as the proximal kidney tubules, submaxillary glands, and intestinal mucosa. Additionally, GNMT is expressed in various neurons located in the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, substantia nigra, and cerebellum, suggesting a potential role in secretion. The properties of GNMT proteins from rabbits, rats, and humans, whether purified from liver or pancreas or expressed in Escherichia coli, have been extensively characterized. All GNMTs exhibit highly similar molecular and kinetic properties. Comparisons of the cDNA and protein sequences of human, rabbit, pig, and rat GNMTs reveal over 84% similarity at the nucleotide level and approximately 90% similarity at the amino acid level. GNMTs are 130 kDa tetramers composed of four identical subunits, each with a molecular weight of 32 kDa. The structures of recombinant rat, mouse, and human GNMTs have been resolved. These tetramers are flat and square, with four nearly spherical subunits arranged around a large central hole. The active sites are located near the center of each subunit. GNMT catalyzes the synthesis of N-methylglycine (sarcosine) from glycine, using S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. It plays a critical role in regulating the ratio of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) to S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) and participates in the detoxification pathway in liver cells. GNMT competes with tRNA methyltransferases for SAM, and its product, SAH, is a potent inhibitor of tRNA methyltransferases but a relatively weak inhibitor of GNMT. By regulating the relative levels of SAM and SAH, GNMT influences cellular methylation capacity, as SAM is the methyl donor for nearly all cellular methylation reactions. An endogenous ligand of GNMT, 5-methyltetrahydropteroylpentaglutamate (5-CH3-H4PteGlu5), is a powerful inhibitor of the enzyme. GNMT has been proposed to link the de novo synthesis of methyl groups to the SAM-to-SAH ratio, thereby bridging methionine and one-carbon metabolism. In addition to its methyltransferase activity, GNMT is identical to the 4S polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH)-binding protein. Its catalytic site resembles a molecular basket, unlike most other SAM-dependent methyltransferases, suggesting that GNMT may capture unidentified chemicals as part of a detoxification process. This unique structure and function indicate that GNMT is a protein with diverse roles. Clinically, GNMT has been shown to detoxify certain environmental carcinogens, such as polyaromatic hydrocarbons and aflatoxin. There is growing evidence supporting the involvement of GNMT deficiency in liver carcinogenesis. The glycoside natural product 1,2,3,4,6-penta-O-galloyl-β-d-glucopyranoside (PGG), isolated from Paeonia lactiflora, an Asian flowering plant, induces GNMT mRNA and protein expression in Huh7 human hepatoma cells.
